日本では「人手不足」が語られる一方、働く人が安心して将来を描ける仕事は十分にあるのだろうか。採用件数や失業率だけでは、雇用の実態は見えない。仕事があっても、収入が低く、契約が短く、技能を伸ばす機会が乏しければ、生活の不安は消えない。
 
かつて日本を支えた終身雇用は、誰もが期待できるものではなくなった。正規雇用者数は増えているものの、非正規雇用者も2025年平均で約2,128万人に上る。有期契約で働く人には、３～４年で契約更新が途絶える不安がある。

Japan is often described as facing a “labor shortage.” Yet are there enough jobs that allow people to plan their futures with confidence? Hiring figures and unemployment rates alone do not reveal the realities of employment. Having a job does not remove financial insecurity if wages are low, contracts are short, and opportunities to develop skills are limited.
 
Lifetime employment, which once supported Japan’s economy, is no longer something everyone can expect. Although the number of regular employees is increasing, non-regular employees also numbered approximately 21.28 million on average in 2025. People on fixed-term contracts face the uncertainty of having their contracts discontinued after three or four years.

Flank just put heavyweight names from inside global legal ops on its new "Orchestration Layer" advisory board. GCs, ops chiefs, partners, people who know where legal work sits inside big companies. All to make sure Flank’s AI agents stay realistic about what actually happens on the ground.

This is the strongest approach I’ve seen yet to wrestle with a problem every AI vendor glosses over: legal work at scale isn’t about process, it’s about edge cases, trust, what happens when the lines blur. The advisors here have handled that at real volume.

But here's what most readers will miss: boards like this aren't cheap and they don't come without real costs, not just in cash but in time and friction. Each new “orchestration” means another layer between a buyer and actual throughput. Supervising these agents, testing what’s new, aligning calendars, none of this is pennies on the dollar compared to just hiring another lawyer. Sometimes the new “AI enabled” workflow is slower, not faster.

I’ve watched the price curve on legal AI go both ways. Right now, adding more quality control often brings the old math back: savings disappear if you still need a team to keep the tech honest. Maybe it works better for intake or front door use cases, but I haven’t seen the breakthrough for end-to-end contract work yet.

We pointed BENCH at a job a real business runs on AI: reading employment contracts against the company's own hiring rules.

Not a public benchmark. Six rules the company actually applies, written down and frozen before anything ran. Then 39 contracts drafted against them. Twelve sit exactly on the limit. 

Probation at precisely six months. Holiday at exactly 28 days. A non-compete paying a token 1 euro that still technically satisfies "must be paid". BENCH ran eleven setups through all of it, same work, same judge.

What I expected: the expensive models win, the cheap ones miss things.

What BENCH found: almost every model found almost every real breach. The difference was entirely in the other direction. They invent problems. Clauses that already met the rule, reported as violations. Every one of those is a contract a lawyer has to re-read for nothing.

The sharpest result was two open-weight models at exactly the same price, $1 per thousand contracts. Qwen3 235B got 38 of 39 right and invented nothing. DeepSeek V3 got 21 of 39 and invented 17. Price told you nothing at all.

Anthropic Claude Haiku looked like the worst of the lot at 26 of 39. Then BENCH showed what it got wrong. All 13 failures were one misreading of a single rule, repeated. It treats "must be paid" as "must be paid in full". That is a sentence in a prompt, not a bad model. Fix it and the cheapest model on the board is suddenly competitive.

That is the part a leaderboard cannot do for you. It ranks models in general. It does not tell you that the cheap one is failing your work for one reason you could fix this afternoon.

BENCH also caught three bugs in our own test harness that were making models look worse than they were. Truncated answers scored as six rule failures. Those are published too, because a benchmark that only reports what makes you look clever is marketing.

This is what we built BENCH for. Not "which model is best". Which setup does your job, and the cheapest way to keep it done.

The April 2026 ServiceNow CSM license packaging redesign is being discussed mostly in terms of cost optimization, but the structural change that matters most for architects is the forced decoupling of service tiers from feature access. The retirement of Standard, Professional, and Enterprise structures means that your licensing strategy is no longer a proxy for your technical architecture.

What few are articulating is that the new tier structure eliminates the old guardrails that prevented you from mixing premium features across customer segments. In the legacy model, if you wanted proactive case deflection with AI for your gold-tier customers, you had to buy up the entire stack. Now, the packaging forces you to be intentional about which capabilities you deploy to which customer segments. This is not a simplification; it is a design constraint that requires you to model your service delivery architecture around consumption units rather than feature bundles.

The most overlooked consequence is on contract governance. With the removal of legacy tiers, you can no longer rely on the platform to enforce feature parity across your customer base. The burden shifts to your architecture to define and enforce service levels at the flow level. I have seen teams deploy a new AI-powered case deflection flow to all customers, only to discover that their licensing only covers it for premium segments. The teams that succeed in 2026 are the ones that embed license-aware routing logic directly into their service operations workflows.

For hiring managers and talent acquisition specialists, the signal to look for is not just CSM certification. It is the ability to answer: how do you ensure that your CSM instance enforces licensing compliance without breaking the customer experience? Someone who can demonstrate they have designed a flow that conditionally enables AI features based on customer tier, or built a custom dashboard that monitors feature consumption against license entitlements, will outperform someone who can only describe the new packaging structure.

The shift toward connected customer service with unified data models means that the line between CSM and ITSM is blurring. If your CSM team is adopting the new packaging in 2026, how are you architecting for license-aware service delivery without adding operational complexity?

SAP licensing isnt exactly a thriller. So we turned it into one. 🔎

Michael Dorn offered several of us masters students at BBW Hochschule the chance to work as interns on real SAP projects and learn from the experts. Apurva Kokane and I took one of them, with Prolona. 

The project: Sherlock, an AI-assisted SAP licensing tool that helps consultants compare converting an on-premise SAP contract against moving to the cloud, department by department. 

Our part: test it with anonymised reports, find bugs and suggest improvements. 

Then came the last question: how do you present your work to a room that has seen a thousand slide decks? We chose to tell it as an animated detective film, followed by a live demo of the real tool.

How we made the presentation:
🎬 The animated film: our own script, with AI-generated characters, scenes and voices 
🖥️ The demo: recorded live, in my own voice

What I took away:
1. Make the complex memorable. A story sticks long after a slide deck is forgotten. 
2. Real projects teach what coursework cant: real data, real feedback and real deadlines. 
3. Teamwork beats tools. Apurva and I only got here by splitting the work and checking each others results. 
4. Presentation is part of the job. Explaining a technical tool clearly is a skill worth practising.

The response in the room was very warm, so were sharing the film below. Thank you Michael Dorn for the opportunity, Leon Mislisch and Dagmar Fischer-Neeb for your guidance, Prolona for the collaboration, and Apurva Kokane for working along with me with me as a colleague. And good luck to my fellow students on their own projects!

"Fractional" now just means "I'm free on Tues/Weds."

That's Gev Marotz, a fractional executive, writing in September. His full line: "Fractional used to mean you owned an outcome. Now it just means 'I'm free on Tues/Weds.'"

The sentence I keep rereading: "The market isn't short on fractional people. It's short on fractional people who say out loud what happens if they don't deliver."

I sell fractional AI leadership. He's describing a real problem in my own market, and I'd rather say it before a client has to.

A week ago Gartner made the same point from the other side. It predicted that by 2028, 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built with vendor help, often by engineers the vendor embeds on site, as costs climb and the customer can't change it without outside help. It also warned about "FDE washing": ordinary consulting relabeled as something special.

So the same failure shows up from 2 directions. Outside help builds something, leaves, and the thing stops working.

My own test for anything I build is boring. Could someone at the client restart it at 4:45 on a Friday without calling me? If not, I'm not done, no matter how good the demo was.

Hiring someone like me is the wrong call when:
You can't name the outcome they own
Nobody inside is learning the system alongside them
The exit plan is "we'll figure it out later"
You need a team of builders, not 1 senior person

Every one of those gaps turns into hours. Somebody on your staff spends them babysitting a tool nobody owns, and none of it gets billed. That's the Non-Billable Leak with a consultant's invoice on top.

Gartner's analyst Mukul Saha listed what a good engagement needs from day one: "governance, business value delivery, IP ownership, project co-ownership, knowledge transfer, and an exit strategy."

Hold any AI help you pay for up to that list, mine included. Circle every item nobody has put in writing.

Send this to whoever signed your last AI contract.

Who tests the AI hiring tool? Right now, nobody is required to. So here's how you test it yourself.

Start with where testing for AI hiring bias stands. New York City has had a bias-audit law for hiring tools since 2023, so the State Comptroller checked how it's going. Two years, two complaints. The city looked at 32 companies and found one problem. The auditors looked at the same 32 and found 17.

Colorado had the broadest AI law in the country until May, when the governor signed a replacement that drops annual impact assessments. The EU moved its high-risk deadlines to late 2027 and 2028.

The pieces exist. NYC requires the auditor. The EU wrote the review. Stanford published the method. What's missing is anyone checking that it happens.

So if you're the one choosing a hiring tool, don't wait for that. I'm not a contracts expert. I've spent over a decade testing products before customers bet on them, and this is the same job. Don't watch their demo. Run yours.

Your cases → their tool → their answers 

The three I'd run first:

1.	Same resume, swap the signals. Name, graduation year, school, clubs. Does the score move?
2.	Ask what it noticed. Did it pick up gender or race, and what did it assume from that? "We don't know" is an honest answer. A made-up one is the test failed.
3.	The human path. Ask what happens when a candidate wants a person. Watch whether anyone in the room knows.

Four more are on the card. Save it. Then ask for the second meeting, because no vendor runs all seven in the first one. The one who books it is the one you want.

What would you add? 👇

Human first, AI second.

The 2026 Data Governance conversation has a blind spot. Everyone is talking about "acculturation" and "federated models," but the structural shift that matters most is the inversion of the governance lifecycle itself.

The old model was reactive: a new dataset arrives, you catalog it, you classify it, you write a policy, and then you enforce it. The latency between arrival and enforcement is where every failure lives. The new model, as confirmed by the latest industry guides, is anticipatory. You embed the governance logic directly into the data's provenance before it ever enters a pipeline. The policy is not applied after the fact. It is inherited.

The non-obvious consequence is that the data catalog is no longer a passive inventory. It is a runtime execution layer. Every field, every schema, every transformation carries its own governance contract. When a query arrives, the system does not check a separate policy database. It reads the contract embedded in the metadata. The governance decision is made at the same speed as the query itself. There is no handoff. There is no review queue.

Here is the practical reality. A team that builds a machine-learning model on customer data in 2026 cannot afford a three-day approval cycle. The model's training window is hours, not days. The teams that succeed are the ones that have stopped treating governance as a separate review gate and started treating it as a pre-compiled set of permissions that are evaluated at line speed. They have moved from policy as a document to policy as a runtime constraint.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the one who can write the most comprehensive governance framework. It is the one who can design the metadata schema that makes policy enforcement a self-executing property of the data itself. I specialize in this. I build the embedded governance layers that let organizations scale regulated data operations without introducing a human-in-the-loop for every access request.

The hardest problem in Data Governance right now is not defining what is allowed. It is engineering a system that can prove, at the exact moment a query executes, that the correct policy was enforced, without adding any measurable latency to the data path. If your organization is scaling AI on sensitive data, what is the one policy you have not yet embedded into your metadata layer that is currently causing your biggest trust gap?
